updates.summary: AI business operators must tell users in advance that a product or service runs on high-impact or generative AI, mark generative AI outputs, and give notice of or mark outputs hard to tell from reality (Art. 31). Operators of AI systems trained with cumulative compute at or above a decree threshold must identify, assess and mitigate risks over the life cycle, monitor and respond to safety incidents and report to the Minister (Art. 32). For high-impact AI, operators must review in advance whether their AI qualifies (Art. 33), take risk management, explanation, user protection and human oversight measures (Art. 34) and endeavour to assess impacts on fundamental rights (Art. 35).
updates.notes: Promulgated on 21 Jan 2025 as Act No. 20676 and in force one year later, on 22 Jan 2026 (Addenda Art. 1); the digital medical device part of Art. 2(4)(d) applies from 24 Jan 2026. Act No. 21311 of 20 Jan 2026 amended it from 22 Jan 2026, renaming the National AI Committee the National AI Strategy Committee (Art. 7); its provisions on AI-vulnerable groups (Art. 3(5)), support for AI use costs (Art. 17-2), a state AI research body (Art. 22-3) and reflecting AI-vulnerable groups in impact assessments (Art. 35(1)) took effect six months after promulgation, on 21 Jul 2026. Art. 12 provides for the AI Safety Institute (KR-01). The Act applies to acts abroad that affect the Korean market or users and excludes decree-designated AI used only for defence or national security (Art. 4). Foreign operators above decree thresholds must designate a domestic agent (Art. 36). Enforcement powers include fact-finding investigations and stop or correction orders (Art. 40); administrative fines of up to KRW 30 million apply for failing to give the prior notice of Art. 31(1), failing to designate a domestic agent, or ignoring such orders (Art. 43).

updates.title: Superior Electoral Court Resolution No. 23,732 of 27 February 2024 amending TSE Resolution No. 23,610 of 18 December 2019 on electoral propaganda
updates.original_title: Resolução nº 23.732, de 27 de fevereiro de 2024 – Altera a Res.-TSE nº 23.610, de 18 de dezembro de 2019, dispondo sobre a propaganda eleitoral
updates.summary: Amends TSE Resolution 23,610/2019 on electoral propaganda. Propaganda using AI-generated synthetic content must say so explicitly, prominently and accessibly, naming the technology. Campaign chatbots and avatars are subject to the same duty and may not simulate dialogue with the candidate or another real person. Deepfakes of a living, deceased or fictitious person's image or voice used to harm or favour a candidacy are banned even with consent, on pain of loss of registration or mandate. Application providers are jointly and severally liable, civilly and administratively, if during the electoral period they do not immediately remove AI-manipulated content breaching the labelling rules.
updates.notes: Adopted on 27 February 2024 (rapporteur Minister Cármen Lúcia) and published in DJE-TSE no. 29 of 4 March 2024, pp. 132-145; in force on publication (Art. 6). Besides the AI rules in new Articles 9-B, 9-C and 9-E, it adds definitions of artificial intelligence and synthetic content to Article 37 of Resolution 23,610/2019 and new duties for application providers (Art. 9-D), including measures against notoriously untrue or seriously decontextualised content and an election-year assessment of their services' impact on the integrity of the electoral process. The labelling duty does not cover image or sound quality adjustments, graphic identity elements and customary campaign photo montages (Art. 9-B § 2).

updates.summary: Would amend the Copyright Act to make it unlawful to share realistic digitally generated imitations of a person's personal characteristics, such as appearance and voice, or of performing artists' performances, without consent. An exception covers caricature, parody, satire and criticism of power and society, but not imitations that are misinformation able to seriously endanger others' rights or essential interests or to create a concrete danger to life or property. The bill also protects performances that are not artistic works, such as improvisations, and aims to secure the right to one's own body and voice and to get the tech giants to take manipulated content down quickly.
updates.notes: Implements the political agreement of 26 June 2025 between the then SVM government (Social Democrats, Venstre and Moderates) and six other parties to create protection against the sharing of digital imitations by amending the Copyright Act. A draft was notified under the EU TRIS procedure as 2025/0654/DK (received 31 October 2025, replacing the withdrawn notification 2025/642/DK; standstill to 3 February 2026, with comments from the Commission). The notified draft would add a Section 73a (personal characteristics) and a Section 65a (performances and artistic presentations) to the Copyright Act, protect both until 50 years after the year of death of the person imitated or the performer, let courts order infringing copies removed from the medium where they are made available, and enter into force on 1 July 2026; its exception did not yet mention danger to life or property. Culture Minister Zenia Stampe introduced the bill on 8 October 2026 and hopes it can enter into force at the turn of the year 2026/27. The bill also changes the rules of the Copyright Licence Tribunal (Ophavsretslicensnævnet) so that the same dispute cannot run before the tribunal and the courts in parallel. The English title is that of the notified draft.

updates.title: Digital Thailand - AI Ethics Guideline
updates.summary: Thailand's AI ethics principles and guidelines, prepared under the Ministry of Digital Economy and Society. They guide AI researchers, designers, developers and service providers in their work, let service recipients know their rights and the risks of AI services, and give state agencies and AI regulators a basis for promoting, supporting and supervising AI, so AI is reliable and secure and benefits people, society and the environment with transparency, inclusiveness and fairness, in line with law, ethics and human rights. After reviewing foreign and corporate frameworks, it sets six principles with guidance under each for state agencies and regulators, developers and providers, and users.
updates.notes: The 46-page document hosted by ETDA is undated. Its cover title is in English only; in its Thai text the document calls itself 'เอกสารหลักการและแนวทางจริยธรรมปัญญาประดิษฐ์' (AI ethics principles and guidelines document). The most recent sources it cites date from 2019, and it refers to the Ministry's strategy for B.E. 2563-2567 (2020-2024). Its six principles are Competitiveness and Sustainability Development; Laws, Ethics and International Standards; Transparency and Accountability; Security and Privacy; Fairness; and Reliability. They were later carried into ETDA's 2023 AI Governance Guideline for Executives. Its review covers OECD, Council of Europe, European Commission, Smart Dubai, Singapore PDPC, Microsoft and Beijing AI principles. The guideline has no enforcement mechanism; Thailand's binding AI framework is still at the stage of the 2026 draft Act on Artificial Intelligence.
